claim: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), claims over 1.6 million lives annually.
source: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), is a major global health concern, claiming over 1.6 million lives annually.
evidence: This is a factual statement about TB mortality that draws from established public health data and knowledge.

claim: Nearly 1.7 billion people globally harbor a dormant Mtb infection.
source: This situation is worsened by the nearly 1.7 billion people globally who harbor a dormant Mtb infection (Houben and Dodd, 2016), coupled with the rising trend of drug-resistant TB cases (World Health Organization, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Houben and Dodd, 2016.

claim: There is a rising trend of drug-resistant TB cases.
source: This situation is worsened by the nearly 1.7 billion people globally who harbor a dormant Mtb infection (Houben and Dodd, 2016), coupled with the rising trend of drug-resistant TB cases (World Health Organization, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization, 2022.

claim: Mtb has the ability to damage the phagosomal membrane, a process that is heavily reliant on the activity of the ESX-1 secretion system.
source: Studies have indicated that Mtb has the ability to damage the phagosomal membrane, a process that is heavily reliant on the activity of the ESX-1 secretion system (Conrad et al., 2017; López-Jiménez et al., 2018; Schnettger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Conrad et al., 2017; López-Jiménez et al., 2018; Schnettger et al., 2017.

claim: ESAT-6 is the most probable candidate driving ESX-1 dependent lytic activity.
source: Currently, the most probable candidate driving ESX-1 dependent lytic activity is the well-known T cell antigen, the 6 kDa early secreted antigenic target (ESAT-6, or EsxA) (Andersen et al., 1995; Sørensen et al., 1995), after which the ESX family of T7SSs was originally named (Gey van Pittius et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andersen et al., 1995; Sørensen et al., 1995; Gey van Pittius et al., 2001.

claim: Many individual ESX-1 component knockouts phenocopy the ESAT-6 deletion, indicating that ESAT-6 itself is responsible for the lion's share of the activity.
source: Secretion of the various ESX-1 substrates are known to be highly complex and interdependent, and while the full scope of ESX-1 components and substrates is still being worked out, many individual ESX-1 component knockouts are known to phenocopy the ESAT-6 deletion, indicating that ESAT-6 itself is responsible for the lion's share of the activity (Chen et al., 2012; Clemmensen et al., 2017; Cronin et al., 2022; Lienard et al., 2020; Sanchez et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2012; Clemmensen et al., 2017; Cronin et al., 2022; Lienard et al., 2020; Sanchez et al., 2020.

claim: Many studies prior to 2017 showing membrane disruption by ESAT-6 were confounded by contamination with the detergent ASB-14.
source: However, the field has been plagued by setbacks such as the discovery that many studies prior to 2017 showing membrane disruption by ESAT-6 were confounded by the contamination with the detergent ASB-14, which was originally added to remove endotoxin (Conrad et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Conrad et al., 2017.

claim: The unique characteristics of Mm compared to Mtb can sometimes lead to differing results, and conclusions drawn from one species do not always apply to the other.
source: However, the unique characteristics of Mm compared to Mtb can sometimes leads to differing results, and conclusions drawn from one species do not always apply to the other (Bosserman et al., 2019; Carlsson et al., 2009; Lienard et al., 2020; Osman et al., 2022; Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bosserman et al., 2019; Carlsson et al., 2009; Lienard et al., 2020; Osman et al., 2022; Smith et al., 2008.

claim: The pMRLB.7 plasmid contains a stretch of 10 additional amino acids ahead of the reported tags.
source: We performed sequencing of both plasmids (Figure 1A), and noticed a stretch of 10 additional amino acids ahead of the reported tags in the pMRLB.7 plasmid (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from plasmid sequencing.

claim: The pMRLB.46 plasmid appears to contain 4 additional amino acids ahead of the expected tag.
source: The precise amino acid sequence of the pMRLB.46 plasmid has not been reported, but it appears to contain 4 additional amino acids ahead of the expected tag.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequencing data.

claim: The full and complete sequences of ESAT-6 and CFP-10 are each contained in their respective plasmids.
source: Importantly, we were able to confirm that the full and complete sequences of ESAT-6 and CFP-10 are each contained in their respective plasmids, and the inconsistencies fall within the C-terminal tag regions of each protein (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental sequencing data.

claim: CFP-10 undergoes N-terminal methionine excision in the E. coli expression system.
source: Amino acid sequences of the recombinant proteins were also confirmed by mass spectrometry (MS), where it was observed that CFP-10 undergoes N-terminal methionine excision in our E. coli expression system (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Giglione et al., 2004; Hirel et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and citations to Giglione et al., 2004; Hirel et al., 1989.

claim: Combining equimolar quantities of ESAT-6 with CFP-10 resulted in a leftward shift in size exclusion chromatography, suggesting correct dimerization.
source: Size exclusion chromatography (SEC) showed appropriate relative retention volumes and combining equimolar quantities of ESAT-6 with CFP-10 resulted in a leftward shift, suggesting correct dimerization (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental SEC data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ESAT-6 and CFP-10 form a 1:1 complex at neutral pH.
source: Combinations of each showed a distinct third band of intermediate charge which was greatest in the 1:1 mixture and absent in each pure protein, indicating formation of a 1:1 complex with no intermediate species.
evidence: This claim is supported by native-PAGE experimental data.

claim: The isoelectric point of ESAT-6 is 5.18 (net charge –8.22 at pH 7.4).
source: The isoelectric point of ESAT-6 and CFP-10 are both quite low, for our constructs they are 5.18 (net charge –8.22 at pH 7.4) and 5.72 (net charge –5.27 at pH 7.4), respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated value based on the protein sequence.

claim: The isoelectric point of CFP-10 is 5.72 (net charge –5.27 at pH 7.4).
source: The isoelectric point of ESAT-6 and CFP-10 are both quite low, for our constructs they are 5.18 (net charge –8.22 at pH 7.4) and 5.72 (net charge –5.27 at pH 7.4), respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated value based on the protein sequence.

claim: Recombinant ESAT-6 produced without detergent was not able to induce hemolysis at any pH between 4.5 and 7.5.
source: Our recombinant ESAT-6 was produced without detergent, and we confirmed that it was not able to induce hemolysis at any pH between 4.5 and 7.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental hemolysis assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mycobacterium marinum (Mm) is capable of efficiently causing hemolysis within 2 hours.
source: Similar to previous reports, we found that Mycobacterium marinum (Mm) is capable of efficiently causing hemolysis within 2 hours (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental hemolysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mtb was incapable of hemolysis over a 2 hour time frame.
source: In contrast, we found that Mtb was incapable of hemolysis over a similar time frame.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental hemolysis data.

claim: Mm-induced hemolysis is ESX-1 dependent.
source: It is well established that Mm-induced hemolysis is ESX-1 dependent, but our results suggest that there are some differences in Mtb that affect the rate or extent of hemolysis.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: One previous study was able to induce hemolysis using Mtb, but this required 48 hr instead of the typical 2.
source: One previous study was able to induce hemolysis using Mtb, but this required 48 hr instead of the typical 2 (Augenstreich et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Augenstreich et al., 2020.

claim: ESAT-6 and CFP-10 preferentially form hetero-oligomers.
source: We first measured the ability of ESAT-6 and CFP-10 to form homo-oligomers or hetero-oligomers (Figure 3B), and found that they preferentially formed hetero-oligomers.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ESAT-6 showed a small, but measurable amount of self-association at neutral pH.
source: ESAT-6 showed a small, but measurable amount of self-association, while CFP-10 showed no self-association.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data.

claim: CFP-10 showed no self-association at neutral pH.
source: ESAT-6 showed a small, but measurable amount of self-association, while CFP-10 showed no self-association.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) of the ESAT-6/CFP-10 heterodimer is 220 pM.
source: We performed a detailed measurement of the ESAT-6/CFP-10 association and measured a KD of 220 pM, indicating exceptionally tight binding (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Renshaw et al., 2002 estimated an upper bound of 10 nM for the dissociation constant of the ESAT-6/CFP-10 heterodimer.
source: The dissociation constant (KD) of the ESAT-6/CFP-10 heterodimer has not hitherto been directly measured, but Renshaw et al., 2002 estimated an upper bound of 10 nM.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Renshaw et al., 2002.

claim: ESAT-6 self-association at neutral pH has an apparent KD of approximately 1.5 µM.
source: The curve shape is suggestive of something other than traditional 1:1 binding, but for comparison purposes we calculated an apparent KD of approximately 1.5 µM, weaker than that of the ESAT-6/CFP-10 association.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data.

claim: The pH of the Mtb-containing compartment typically ranges from 4.5 in IFN-γ activated macrophages to 6.2 in non-activated macrophages.
source: The pH of the Mtb-containing compartment typically ranges from 4.5 in IFN-γ activated macrophages to 6.2 in non-activated macrophages (MacMicking et al., 2003; Vandal et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to MacMicking et al., 2003; Vandal et al., 2008.

claim: ESAT-6 displayed robust self-association at pH 4.5.
source: Surprisingly, ESAT-6 displayed robust self-association at pH 4.5 (Figure 3E), resulting in several-fold more mass attaching to the sensor than even the ESAT-6/CFP-10 association at neutral pH.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Low pH conditions trigger ESAT-6 to assemble into larger complexes.
source: The apparent KD for this interaction was slightly weaker than ESAT-6 self-association at neutral pH, but the total amount of binding was 20–30-fold greater, suggesting that low pH conditions trigger ESAT-6 to assemble into larger complexes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from BLI experimental data showing increased binding at low pH.

claim: ESAT-6 and CFP-10 maintain a stable interaction at low-pH.
source: Our results support the stable interaction of ESAT-6 and CFP-10 at low-pH (Figure 3F), which exhibits an extremely tight apparent KD of 0.4 pM at pH 4.5: however, this is likely due to the multivalent ESAT-6 self-association occurring in this condition (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: pH 5.0 was the most basic pH at which increased ESAT-6 self-association occurred.
source: To determine the precise pH at which ESAT-6 self-association becomes dominant, we performed BLI experiments at half pH units from 4.5 to 6.5 (Figure 3H). We found that 5.0 was the most basic pH at which increased self-association occurred.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: An increase in turbidity was observed at pH 4.5 but not 7.5 which was greater for ESAT-6 than CFP-10.
source: We observed an increase in turbidity at pH 4.5 but not 7.5 which was greater for ESAT-6 than CFP-10, in line with previous findings (De Leon et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by turbidity assay data and a citation to De Leon et al., 2012.

claim: Fluorescence microscopy shows the development of individual strands with the appearance of a heavily kinked thread or beads on a string for ESAT-6 complexes at pH 4.5.
source: Fluorescence microscopy shows the development of individual strands with the appearance of a heavily kinked thread or beads on a string (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ESAT-6 strand structures were not present at neutral pH or when 6 M guanidine was added to acidified ESAT-6.
source: These structures were not present at neutral pH or when 6 M guanidine was added to acidified ESAT-6.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: At pH 7.5, ESAT-6 exists as a single peak with an approximate molecular weight of 21 kDa, which most likely corresponds to an ESAT-6 homodimer.
source: At pH 7.5, we observed a single peak with an approximate molecular weight of 21 kDa, which most likely corresponds to an ESAT-6 homodimer (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No monomeric ESAT-6 was observed at pH 7.5, indicating that it likely self-pairs in the absence of CFP-10.
source: We did not observe the presence of any monomeric ESAT-6, indicating that it likely self-pairs in the absence of CFP-10.
evidence: This claim is inferred from SEC-MALS data showing no monomer peak.

claim: At pH 4.5, ESAT-6 forms a single, well-defined peak at 46 kDa, most likely corresponding to a tetramer.
source: At pH 4.5, we were surprised to see a single, well-defined peak at 46 kDa, most likely corresponding to a tetramer (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No measurable monomer, dimer, or higher molecular weight complexes were observed for ESAT-6 at pH 4.5 by SEC-MALS.
source: No measurable monomer, dimer, or higher molecular weight complexes were observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS experimental data.

claim: The energy-minimized structure of monomeric ESAT-6 strongly resembles its conformation in the heterodimer.
source: We observed that the energy-minimized structure of monomeric ESAT-6 strongly resembles its conformation in the heterodimer.
evidence: This claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The helix-turn-helix structure of ESAT-6 exhibits strong amphipathic nature, with both helices aligning to form a hydrophobic face flanked by charged residues.
source: The helix-turn-helix structure exhibits strong amphipathic nature, with both helices aligning to form a hydrophobic face flanked by charged residues (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is based on molecular modeling data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The ESAT-6 homodimer model showed head-to-tail alignment of the ESAT-6 monomers associating via their hydrophobic faces and stabilized on either side by salt bridges.
source: The homodimer model showed head-to-tail alignment of the ESAT-6 monomers associating via their hydrophobic faces and stabilized on either side by salt bridges (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is based on molecular modeling data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In the ESAT-6 tetramer model, dimers interact in a head-to-tail orientation via their hydrophilic faces, supported by salt bridges.
source: We observed the dimers interacting in a head-to-tail orientation via their hydrophilic faces, supported by salt bridges (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is based on molecular modeling data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: At pH 7.5, the average RMSF of the ESAT-6 monomer is 2.51, which reduces to 2.33 for the dimer.
source: At pH 7.5, the average RMSF of the monomer is 2.51, which reduces to 2.33 for the dimer due to the reduced flexibility between residues 20 and 50.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: At pH 4.5, the RMSF is 2.74, 2.04, and 1.94 for the ESAT-6 monomer, dimer, and tetramer, respectively.
source: At pH 4.5, the difference between each state is even more pronounced, with an RMSF of 2.74, 2.04, and 1.94 for the monomer, dimer, and tetramer, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: E11rv bound to ESAT-6 with a KD of 331 nM.
source: E11rv bound similarly to ESAT-6 and ESAT-6-LPETG with KDs of 331 nM and 376 nM, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data.

claim: E11rv bound to ESAT-6-LPETG with a KD of 376 nM.
source: E11rv bound similarly to ESAT-6 and ESAT-6-LPETG with KDs of 331 nM and 376 nM, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI experimental data.

claim: E11rv binding to ESAT-6 results in decreased deuteration around positions 50–65 and increased deuteration in the region between residues 66 to 94.
source: For E11rv, we observed decreased deuteration compared to apo around positions 50–65 (on the C-terminal helix, near the loop), and to a lesser extent positions 98–110 (within the tag). The region between these segments, from residues 66 to 94, displayed an increase in solvent exposure, as did residues 14–28, on the opposing helix directly across from 66 to 94.
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrogen-deuterium exchange experimental data.

claim: E11rv binds around residues 50–65 of ESAT-6.
source: A likely explanation for this pattern is that E11rv binds around residues 50–65, and that this somehow destabilizes the C-terminal portion of the helix or separates the helices enough to allow more solvent exposure between helices.
evidence: This claim is inferred from HDX-MS data.

claim: E11rv led to a statistically significant reduction in Mtb viability in THP-1 cells.
source: In this experiment, we found that E11rv led to a statistically significant reduction in Mtb viability (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the live/dead reporter assay shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: E11rv reduced the growth rate of luminescent Mtb in THP-1 cells substantially.
source: We then infected the nanobody-expressing THP-1 cells with luminescent Mtb and monitored their growth continuously via plate reader for 5 days, and we found that E11rv reduced the growth rate substantially (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the luminescence growth assay shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Over 5 days, isotype-expressing cells allowed Mtb to grow to sixfold over its starting value while E11rv-expressing cells reduced this to just under threefold.
source: Over the full 5 days, the isotype-expressing cells allowed the Mtb to grow to sixfold over its starting value while the E11rv-expressing cells reduced this to just under threefold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the luminescence growth assay.

claim: ESAT-6 undergoes rapid self-association into large complexes at pH levels below 5.0.
source: This study has several key findings. Firstly, ESAT-6 undergoes rapid self-association into large complexes at pH levels below 5.0, and this may be preceded by formation of stable tetramers.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data including BLI, turbidity, microscopy, and SEC-MALS.

claim: ESAT-6 self-association at low pH may be preceded by formation of stable tetramers.
source: This study has several key findings. Firstly, ESAT-6 undergoes rapid self-association into large complexes at pH levels below 5.0, and this may be preceded by formation of stable tetramers.
evidence: This claim is inferred from SEC-MALS data showing tetramers at pH 4.5.

claim: In the absence of CFP-10, ESAT-6 exists as a homodimer at neutral pH.
source: Second, in the absence of CFP-10, ESAT-6 exists as a homodimer at neutral pH.
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS data.

claim: E11rv can inhibit the growth of Mtb inside cells when treated externally or via cytoplasmic expression.
source: Third, our nanobody, E11rv, binds to ESAT-6 and can inhibit the growth of Mtb inside cells when treated externally or via cytoplasmic expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both the live/dead reporter assay and the luminescence growth assay.

claim: ESAT-6 may still be able to self-associate within membranes via its hydrophilic face.
source: This implies that ESAT-6 may still be able to self-associate within membranes via its hydrophilic face.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on modeling data showing two interaction interfaces.

claim: Low pH is required for ESAT-6 self-association at the hydrophilic interface.
source: This agrees with the putative requirement for compartment acidification in order to drive membrane damage, as our data suggests that low pH is required for self-association at this interface, but likely does not affect the hydrophobic interface, which must then require a different mechanism for dissociation and membrane insertion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing pH-dependent self-association.

claim: Other mycobacterial factors may help facilitate the membrane insertion of ESAT-6, such as phthiocerol dimycocerosates.
source: Some have suggested that other mycobacterial factors may help facilitate the membrane insertion of ESAT-6, such as phthiocerol dimycocerosates (Augenstreich et al., 2020; Augenstreich et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Augenstreich et al., 2020; Augenstreich et al., 2017.

claim: A recent study demonstrated a pentameric EsxE/EsxF structure capable of membrane insertion and toxin trafficking.
source: However, there is precedent for ESAT-6-like WXG proteins to form organized membrane channels, with a recent study demonstrating a pentameric EsxE/EsxF structure capable of membrane insertion and toxin trafficking (Tak et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tak et al., 2021.

claim: EsxE does not dissociate from EsxF in order to insert into the membrane.
source: Critically, EsxE does not dissociate from EsxF in order to insert into the membrane.
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about EsxE/EsxF.

claim: E11rv showed functional effects both when added in the media and when expressed inside the cell cytoplasm, suggesting a significant amount of communication between Mtb inside the phagosome and other compartments of the cell.
source: Because E11rv showed functional effects both when added in the media and when expressed inside the cell cytoplasm, it suggests a significant amount of communication between Mtb inside the phagosome and other compartments of the cell.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing E11rv effects in both conditions.

claim: ESAT-6 has been shown to induce apoptosis.
source: This is consistent with the findings of many other studies which show numerous putative activities for ESAT-6 such as induction of apoptosis (Behura et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2015), inhibition of interferon-γ production (Kumar et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2011), inhibition of autophagy (Dong et al., 2016; Romagnoli et al., 2012; Yabaji et al., 2020), inhibition of antigen presentation (Sreejit et al., 2014), induction of type I interferon (Jang et al., 2018; Lienard et al., 2020), and a more recent study showing an ESX-1-dependent mechanism for incorporation of Mtb antigens into MHC-I presentation via cytosolic antigen processing (Leddy et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Behura et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2015.

claim: ESAT-6 has been shown to inhibit interferon-γ production.
source: This is consistent with the findings of many other studies which show numerous putative activities for ESAT-6 such as induction of apoptosis (Behura et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2015), inhibition of interferon-γ production (Kumar et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2011), inhibition of autophagy (Dong et al., 2016; Romagnoli et al., 2012; Yabaji et al., 2020), inhibition of antigen presentation (Sreejit et al., 2014), induction of type I interferon (Jang et al., 2018; Lienard et al., 2020), and a more recent study showing an ESX-1-dependent mechanism for incorporation of Mtb antigens into MHC-I presentation via cytosolic antigen processing (Leddy et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kumar et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2011.

claim: ESAT-6 has been shown to inhibit autophagy.
source: This is consistent with the findings of many other studies which show numerous putative activities for ESAT-6 such as induction of apoptosis (Behura et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2015), inhibition of interferon-γ production (Kumar et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2011), inhibition of autophagy (Dong et al., 2016; Romagnoli et al., 2012; Yabaji et al., 2020), inhibition of antigen presentation (Sreejit et al., 2014), induction of type I interferon (Jang et al., 2018; Lienard et al., 2020), and a more recent study showing an ESX-1-dependent mechanism for incorporation of Mtb antigens into MHC-I presentation via cytosolic antigen processing (Leddy et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2016; Romagnoli et al., 2012; Yabaji et al., 2020.

claim: ESAT-6 has been shown to inhibit antigen presentation.
source: This is consistent with the findings of many other studies which show numerous putative activities for ESAT-6 such as induction of apoptosis (Behura et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2015), inhibition of interferon-γ production (Kumar et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2011), inhibition of autophagy (Dong et al., 2016; Romagnoli et al., 2012; Yabaji et al., 2020), inhibition of antigen presentation (Sreejit et al., 2014), induction of type I interferon (Jang et al., 2018; Lienard et al., 2020), and a more recent study showing an ESX-1-dependent mechanism for incorporation of Mtb antigens into MHC-I presentation via cytosolic antigen processing (Leddy et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sreejit et al., 2014.

claim: ESAT-6 has been shown to induce type I interferon.
source: This is consistent with the findings of many other studies which show numerous putative activities for ESAT-6 such as induction of apoptosis (Behura et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2015), inhibition of interferon-γ production (Kumar et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2011), inhibition of autophagy (Dong et al., 2016; Romagnoli et al., 2012; Yabaji et al., 2020), inhibition of antigen presentation (Sreejit et al., 2014), induction of type I interferon (Jang et al., 2018; Lienard et al., 2020), and a more recent study showing an ESX-1-dependent mechanism for incorporation of Mtb antigens into MHC-I presentation via cytosolic antigen processing (Leddy et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jang et al., 2018; Lienard et al., 2020.

claim: A recent study showed an ESX-1-dependent mechanism for incorporation of Mtb antigens into MHC-I presentation via cytosolic antigen processing.
source: This is consistent with the findings of many other studies which show numerous putative activities for ESAT-6 such as induction of apoptosis (Behura et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2015), inhibition of interferon-γ production (Kumar et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2011), inhibition of autophagy (Dong et al., 2016; Romagnoli et al., 2012; Yabaji et al., 2020), inhibition of antigen presentation (Sreejit et al., 2014), induction of type I interferon (Jang et al., 2018; Lienard et al., 2020), and a more recent study showing an ESX-1-dependent mechanism for incorporation of Mtb antigens into MHC-I presentation via cytosolic antigen processing (Leddy et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leddy et al., 2023.

claim: ESAT-6 may get into the cytoplasm via disruptions in the phagosomal membrane to establish two-way communication between compartments, or by complete phagosomal escape of Mtb into the cytoplasm and subsequent secretion of ESAT-6 directly into the cytoplasm.
source: Most of these functions rely on ESAT-6 getting into the cytoplasm, and this may occur via disruptions in the phagosomal membrane to establish two-way communication between compartments, or by complete phagosomal escape of Mtb into the cytoplasm and subsequent secretion of ESAT-6 directly into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing possible mechanisms for ESAT-6 cytoplasmic access.

claim: Using three molar equivalents of labeling reagent, ESAT-6 was obtained with an average of 0.99 biotins/protein.
source: Using three molar equivalents of labeling reagent, we obtained ESAT-6 with an average of 0.99 biotins/protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental biotinylation data.

claim: ESAT-6 normally contains three lysines, and the pMRLB.7 construct contains one additional lysine for a total of four.
source: ESAT-6 normally contains three lysines, and the pMRLB.7 construct contains one additional lysine for a total of four (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ESAT-6 is approximately 38% demethionylated while CFP-10 is fully demethionylated.
source: ESAT-6 is approximately 38% demethionylated while CFP-10 is fully demethionylated.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The pMRLB.7 and pMRLB.46 plasmids have been used extensively in literature, including many of the most influential biochemical characterization studies.
source: Both of these plasmids have been used extensively in literature, including many of the most influential biochemical characterization studies (Augenstreich et al., 2020; Behura et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2010; Conrad et al., 2017; de Jonge et al., 2007; Eitson et al., 2012; Gallegos et al., 2008; Harrison et al., 2014; Koyuncu et al., 2021; Lim et al., 2016; Mukherjee et al., 2007; Niazi et al., 2015; Osman et al., 2022; Pathak et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2011; Refai et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2008; Stavri et al., 2012; Vesosky et al., 2010; Woolhiser et al., 2007; Xiao et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using these plasmids.

claim: The specification sheet for pMRLB.7 indicates that it includes a C-terminal FALE solubility tag and subsequent Histidine affinity tag.
source: The specification sheet for pMRLB.7 indicates that it includes a C-terminal FALE solubility tag and subsequent Histidine affinity tag while pMRLB.46 indicates that it contains only a C-terminal Histidine tag.
evidence: This claim is based on information from the plasmid specification sheet.

claim: The specification sheet for pMRLB.46 indicates that it contains only a C-terminal Histidine tag.
source: The specification sheet for pMRLB.7 indicates that it includes a C-terminal FALE solubility tag and subsequent Histidine affinity tag while pMRLB.46 indicates that it contains only a C-terminal Histidine tag.
evidence: This claim is based on information from the plasmid specification sheet.

claim: Mtb utilizes a plethora of virulence factors delivered via its several ESX-secretion systems to successfully establish an infection in the host.
